implementation_notes: Foundation already ships the facade: FileHandle is documented as an object-oriented wrapper for a file descriptor whose creation methods take ownership of the descriptor and close it when the object is deallocated, and URLSession wraps the network stack the same way. Reuse those, keep the teardown explicit where the error matters (close() in a defer), and let ARC/deinit be the backstop rather than the plan; a hand-written class is warranted when the resource is a C library (see the C-interop variant).
pitfalls: deinit is the backstop, not the plan: an object captured by a long-lived closure keeps the descriptor open, and an error from closing inside deinit is lost.
FileHandle reads and writes block the calling thread; the async variants rely on a run loop, so a facade over them must respect the threading model.
Foundation's behaviour differs between Apple platforms and the open-source corelibs implementation, which has used fatalError on I/O failure paths - verify error handling on each target.

variants.name: Swift class over an imported C module
variants.idiom_name: class owning OpaquePointer, released in deinit
variants.implementation_notes: Swift imports a C library directly through a module map, so no bridge layer is needed: a class stores the OpaquePointer (or UnsafeMutableRawPointer) returned by the create function, calls the C functions from its methods, translates return codes into thrown Swift errors, and releases the handle in deinit with close() available for deterministic release. Strings and buffers cross through withCString/withUnsafeBufferPointer, and the wrapper is the only place that knows the pointer is not null until deinit.
pitfalls: The OpaquePointer must not escape the class: anything kept past deinit points at freed native memory.
Swift structs have no deinit, so a handle-owning facade has to be a class (or a ~Copyable struct with deinit on newer toolchains).
Pointers borrowed from withCString/withUnsafeBufferPointer are only valid inside the call, and a C callback into Swift needs an unmanaged context object to stay alive.
